newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila rights group howls as mayor paints town red.
newsitem.headline: Manila rights group howls as mayor paints town red.

text.p: First, he swept through Manila's notorious red light district. Now, he's painting the doors of drug dealers red.
Human rights groups, however, are seeing red, too.

"No matter whose toes I step on, I go for broke," Alfredo Lim, the brass-knuckled mayor of the Philippines' premier city, said as he led policemen into tough neighbourhoods to paint houses of suspected drug dealers with signs such as, "A pusher lives here, get out."
"Warning! Drug protector. Beat it!" was a message Lim's men sprayed on the door of one of three homes owned by a fellow policeman arrested for trying for the release of a jailed pusher.

Lim's unorthodox methods have raised the hackles of the country's Human Rights Commission and a lawyers group, which asked the Supreme Court last week to declare the mayor's campaign unconstitutional.
They called Lim's methods "chilling" and said it smacked of Adolf Hitler's campaign of branding the homes of Jews with the Star of David.

"Let us have daily or weekly executions (of drug pushers) if the situation permits. But let those who will face the full fury of justice enjoy due process... We might as well hand this country over to savages," the Manila Standard newspaper said.
"DIRTY HARRY" OF THE PHILIPPINES

Dubbed the "Dirty Harry" of the Philippines -- after the trigger-happy Hollywood detective played by actor Clint Eastwood -- for his strong-arm tactics in dealing with criminals, Lim seems genuinely amazed that anyone should find anything wrong with what he is doing.
"What is the beef about these violations of human rights?," he told Reuters. "What rights have I violated? How about the rights of these victims (of) these drug pushers?
"Shall we just close our eyes to this problem?"

Told by Human Rights Commissioner Nasser Marohomsalic in a public debate that criminals also had a right to dignity, Lim countered: "How about the dignity of the victims that was devastated? I don't believe it's the right of a drug pusher to destroy the future of another person.
"What I am doing is no different from what you'd do if you had a savage dog in your house. You would hang the sign 'beware of dogs'."
TOUGH ANTI-DRUG LAWS
Tough anti-drug laws in the Philippines impose the death penalty on anyone possessing at least 200 grams of methamphetamine crystals, widely called "ice", or at least 40 gm of cocaine or heroine.
But Lim says legal loopholes that allow pushers to post bail if they are found carrying less than those amounts have enabled them to continue with their trade.
"This is like a circus, a merry-go-round. You arrest a pusher in the morning, he posts bail in the afternoon, the same night he starts pushing again."
While he has critics, the silver-haired, 67-year-old Lim nevertheless has won wide support for his campaign.
The former police general endeared himself to the largely conservative Roman Catholic church when he shut down the Ermita "red light" district after being elected mayor in 1992.
An outbreak of cholera that killed seven Manila residents last year sent him on the warpath again.
Blaming the epidemic on flies and cockroaches, he gave cash to housewives and children who captured the insects. For a rat, he paid more.
"At least Lim's vandalism is for a worthy cause," political scientist Alex Magno said of the "scarlet-letter" campaign. "And we can't quarrel with its sheer inventiveness.
"He has put an entirely new meaning to the phrase 'painting the town red'."
Official statistics on the extent of drug addiction in the capital seem to back Lim's hard-nosed tactics.

Twenty percent of more than 600,000 high school students have used methamphetamine drugs, while another 4.5 percent have tried marijuana. Among 540,000 college students, almost 100,000 have used one of the two drugs.

Manila newspapers have likened Lim's campaign to the branding of fictional American adulteress Hester Prynne with the letter "A" on her chest, or the shaving of the heads of European women who collaborated with German troops during World War Two.
His campaign has shown success. Sixty percent of the occupants of more than 200 houses he has branded since July 1 have fled the city, Lim said.

"We'll get there. Don't be impatient," he said, dismissing criticism that he is targeting only the lowly pushers in shanty towns and has not gone after the big drug lords or influential politicians alleged to protect them.
"Nobody is above the law... There are no sacred cows here," he said.
